Several coronal and heliospheric models have been installed and/or recently upgraded at the Community Coordinated Modeling Center (CCMC), including the Wang-Sheely-Arge (WSA)-Enlil model, MHD-Around-a-Sphere (MAS)-Enlil model, Space Weather Modeling Framework (SWMF), and heliospheric tomography using interplanetary scintillation data. Ulysses recorded the last fast latitudinal scan from southern to northern poles in 2007. By comparing the modeling results with Ulysses observations over seven Carrington rotations, we have extended our third-party validation from the previous near-Earth solar wind to middle to high latitudes, in the same late declining phase of solar cycle 23. Besides visual comparison, we have quantitatively assessed the models’ capabilities in reproducing the time series, statistics, and latitudinal variations of solar wind parameters for a speciﬁc range of model parameter settings, inputs, and grid conﬁgurations available at CCMC. The WSA-Enlil model results vary with three different magnetogram inputs. The MAS-Enlil model captures the solar wind parameters well, despite its underestimation of the speed at middle to high latitudes. The new version of SWMF misses many solar wind variations probably because it uses lower grid resolution than other models. The interplanetary scintillation-tomography cannot capture the latitudinal variations of solar wind well yet. Because the model performance varies with parameter settings which are optimized for different epochs or ﬂow states, the performance metric study provided here can serve as a template that researchers can use to validate the models for the time periods and conditions of interest to them. 1. As an outsider of the modeling teams, a user is often left wondering about the reliability of these models and which one to choose. As suggested by the analysis above, we divide the solar wind into two regions: low latitudes (within ±30°) and middle to high latitudes (30°–60° in each hemisphere). The search located the paper but did not return its RMSE figures, so I can't confirm those numbers from these results.

- **The paper:** Gressl et al. (2014), "Comparative Study of MHD Modeling of the Background Solar Wind," appeared in Solar Physics vol. 289, pp. 1783–1801 (per a reference list on Springer). It is also on arXiv as 1312.1220.
- **Models compared:** The authors tested MAS/ENLIL, WSA/ENLIL, and MAS/MAS against in-situ data from ACE and Wind at 1 AU, using 2007 as a low-activity year.
- **Main findings:** All models reproduced the general structure of the background wind. Solar wind speed was the best-matched parameter. Arrival times of high-speed streams were off by roughly one day. The choice of synoptic magnetic map significantly affected performance.
- **Secondary citation:** A later paper (arXiv 1607.07048) summarizes Gressl et al. as finding the same broad agreement, with stream arrival errors of about one day.

To get the RMSE values for the ENLIL, MAS, and ESWF comparisons, the full text is at arxiv.org/abs/1312.1220 or ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1312.1220. I did not see "ESWF" mentioned in any of these results, so check whether that term appears in the paper itself.

The search didn't surface the RMSE figures from the paper. The results confirm the paper's basics and describe its scope, but none of the snippets report an RMSE value.

- **Paper details:** MacNeice's 2009 paper in *Space Weather* (vol. 7, S12002, doi:10.1029/2009SW000489) is the second in a series on independent validation of community models. It presents a validation of the WSA model meant to serve as a baseline for later models. (Sources: [1-2], [1-6], [8-6])
- **Context:** The WSA model is used by several agencies to forecast solar wind conditions at Earth up to four days ahead, which is the motivation for the systematic validation. (Source: [1-3])
- **Model version:** The CCMC workshop slides from 2010 list the validated version as WSA v1.6 and describe its three-part structure and inputs from synoptic magnetograms. (Source: [5-1], [5-3])
- **Related work:** A companion MacNeice 2009 paper on identifying events in model timelines used the same WSA version and Carrington rotations 1650 onward. (Source: [4-10], [4-16])

To get the RMSE values, I'd suggest opening the full paper through the AGU site or the NASA NTRS PDF (https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20110007820/downloads/20110007820.pdf), since the text in the search snippets is garbled in places and the tables weren't captured.

I didn't find the 2023 *Space Weather* paper by Milošić in these results, so I can't confirm its findings. The results do cover related EUHFORIA validation work on high-speed streams:

- **Background wind validation:** Hinterreiter et al. compared the basic EUHFORIA 1.0.4 setup against ACE measurements for 2008 (low activity) and 2012 (high activity). They found a better match between model results and observations in the low-activity phase, and the quality of the modeled solar-wind parameters is found to be rather variable.
- **Event-based tests:** The same validation effort applied established test methods to continuous variables and to event-based measures such as the arrival time and impact speed of solar wind high speed streams (HSS).
- **Underestimated speeds:** Earlier EUHFORIA results indicated that the velocities of both the slow and fast solar wind are frequently underestimated.
- **Coronal model comparison:** A later study swapped in the MULTI-VP coronal model and compared it with the default WSA model for two HSS cases where the standard EUHFORIA setup failed to reproduce the HSS plasma and magnetic signatures at Earth. It used GONG and WSO magnetograms to separate effects of the coronal model from effects of the input data.
